title: Given a binary tree where each node has an extra `next` pointer, connect each node to its immediate right neighbor on the same level. The last node of each level should point to null.
shortTitle: Connect Level Order Siblings (Populate Next Right Pointers per Level)

s1_definition.profdef: Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot. While draining a level, keep a reference to the previously dequeued node and set `previous.next = currentNode`; the first node of each level has no left neighbor, and the last node's `next` stays null by default. After processing, each level forms a left-to-right linked list via `next`.
s1_definition.analogy: In the National Bank of India approval tree, every approver on a rank should know who sits to their immediate right on the same rank, so a request can slide sideways along a rank. You walk each rank left to right and clip each approver to the next one on that rank.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; within a level, link each node's `next` to the node dequeued right after it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot. While draining a level, keep a reference to the previously dequeued node and set `previous.next = currentNode`; the first node of each level has no left neighbor, and the last node's `next` stays null by default. After processing, each level forms a left-to-right linked list via `next`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** In the National Bank of India approval tree, every approver on a rank should know who sits to their immediate right on the same rank, so a request can slide sideways along a rank. You walk each rank left to right and clip each approver to the next one on that rank.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; within a level, link each node's `next` to the node dequeued right after it.

sections.s2_technical:
The level-size snapshot isolates each level. While draining, maintain a `previous` pointer initialized to null at the start of each level. For each dequeued node, if `previous` is not null set `previous.next = node`, then set `previous = node`. Enqueue children as usual. At the level's end, the last node's `next` remains null because nothing follows it. This wires each level into a singly linked chain through the `next` field.

For example a perfect tree level [4,5,6,7] ends with 4.next=5, 5.next=6, 6.next=7, 7.next=null. The connections are built purely from dequeue order, which is already left to right.

A senior-level nuance is that this BFS solution uses O(w) queue space, whereas the famous follow-up achieves O(1) extra space by using the `next` pointers already built on the current level to traverse and wire the next level without a queue. For a perfect binary tree that O(1) approach is expected at senior level; for a general tree the queue-based version is the robust, clearly correct choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants horizontal routing across each rank of its approval tree so a stalled request can be handed to the approver immediately to the right on the same rank without going back up to a parent. Each node needs a `next` pointer to its right sibling-level neighbor. This is exactly connect-level-order-siblings: BFS and link each node to the next within its level.

The code contains a `LevelNode` with a `next` field, a `SiblingConnector` with `connect(root)`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: perfect tree, root 1; level 2 is 2,3; level 3 is 4,5,6,7.

Step 1: Level 1 has only node 1. previous starts null, so no link is set; 1.next stays null. Enqueue 2,3.

Step 2: Level 2 drains 2 then 3. For 2, previous is null, so no link; previous becomes 2. For 3, previous is 2, so 2.next=3; previous becomes 3. 3.next stays null. Enqueue 4,5,6,7.

Step 3: Level 3 drains 4,5,6,7. Links set: 4.next=5, 5.next=6, 6.next=7; 7.next stays null.

Step 4: Each level is now a left-to-right chain.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Level chain: 1 -> null
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Level chain: 2 -> 3 -> null
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Level chain: 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> null
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: perfect tree rooted at 1
    │
    ▼
  SiblingConnector.connect()  (queue + previous per level)
    │ L1: 1 -> null
    │ L2: 2 -> 3 -> null
    │ L3: 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> null
    ▼
  Output: each level linked via next
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connecting level order siblings means giving every node a next pointer to its immediate right neighbor on the same level, and I solve it with Tree BFS and the level-size snapshot. As I drain each level I keep a previous pointer, reset to null at the start of every level, and for each node I set the previous node's next to the current node before advancing previous. Because the dequeue order within a level is already left to right, this wires each level into a singly linked chain, and the last node of each level naturally keeps a null next because nothing follows it.

I always mention the famous follow-up: the queue-based solution uses space proportional to the widest level, but for a perfect binary tree there is an elegant constant-space version that reuses the next pointers already established on the current level to stitch the next level without any queue at all. At senior level the interviewer often expects that O(1) approach, while the queue version remains the robust, obviously correct choice for a general tree.

In my work at the National Bank of India this enabled horizontal routing across each rank of the approval tree, so a stalled request could be handed to the approver immediately to the right on the same rank instead of bubbling back up to a parent. Building the next pointers level by level with the previous-node linking gave exactly that sideways navigation.
